summary: A modular monolith build: Next.js on the frontend, Python + Django for the backend, PostgreSQL for data, hosted on DigitalOcean for about $207-623 a month. It keeps data in India under DPDP, builds on the team's Python, pushes live updates, and ships as one deployable that a team of 3 can build in 8 weeks.

frontend.choice: Next.js (React) + React Native (Expo) for the Android app
frontend.justification: Next.js (React) is the frontend for an E-commerce / marketplace project with about 6,000 daily users (~12 requests/s at peak), built by a team of 3 in 8 weeks. Search visibility is marked critical (organic traffic is the business), and it serves full HTML from the server or the build (SEO 5.0/5), so crawlers read the content without running JavaScript. It leads the runner-up, Nuxt (Vue), by 2.3 stack points (points of the overall stack score, the average of the four layer scores). You also target iOS/Android. React Native (Expo) scored best among mobile toolkits with the same weights and backend; it shares skills/types with Next.js (React).

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 2.3 points. Next.js (React) is stronger on development speed (5.0 vs 4.0), ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 4.0); Nuxt (Vue) is stronger on learning curve (4.0 vs 3.0), portability (low lock-in) (5.0 vs 4.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 5.5 points. Next.js (React) is stronger on SEO (5.0 vs 2.0), development speed (5.0 vs 4.0); React SPA (Vite) is stronger on low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0), learning curve (4.0 vs 3.0); React SPA (Vite) takes a penalty: Client-side rendering is a liability when organic search is the business.
Ruled out: Mobile toolkit; web is a target, so the primary frontend is a web framework (mobile app suggested as companion)
Ruled out: Mobile toolkit; web is a target, so the primary frontend is a web framework (mobile app suggested as companion)

tradeoffs: App Router + Server Components add conceptual load
Some features (ISR, image optimisation, middleware) are smoothest on Vercel

backend.justification: Python + Django serves the API at about 12 requests/s at peak (Medium (500-5,000 users online at once)) for a team of 3. The team lists Python, so it needs no new server language (team skill match 4.5/5). It runs as a long-running Python service, so background jobs, WebSockets and database connection pools live in one deployable process. Python + FastAPI is within 0.1 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied); Python + Django has the higher stack score.

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.1 points lower; either is defensible. Python + Django is stronger on ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 4.0), structure for large teams (4.0 vs 2.0); Python + FastAPI is stronger on realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0), performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 1.4 points. Python + Django is stronger on development speed (5.0 vs 4.0), structure for large teams (4.0 vs 1.0); Node.js + Express is stronger on realtime fit (4.0 vs 2.0), team skill match (5.0 vs 4.5).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 10.5 points. Python + Django is stronger on team skill match (4.5 vs 1.5), development speed (5.0 vs 3.0); Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot is stronger on scalability (5.0 vs 4.0), realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0); Java/Kotlin + Spring Boot takes a penalty: Nobody on the team listed Java/Kotlin or a closely related skill: a new server language to learn.
Ruled out: Only for read-only sites; your users sign in, post or pay

tradeoffs: Realtime fit is only 2.0/5 (weight 1.2).
Realtime needs Django Channels + Redis
Sync-first ORM; async support is partial

database.justification: Your data is mainly relational and reaches about 34 GB within 12 months; PostgreSQL fits relational data 5/5. Strong consistency is assumed, since no input says stale reads are acceptable, and PostgreSQL gives it: a read after a write always sees that write. Its share of the estimated bill is $75-$150 a month, against a total budget of $150 a month. MySQL is within 0.3 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied); PostgreSQL has the higher stack score.

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.3 points lower; either is defensible. PostgreSQL is stronger on realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 6.4 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on data-model fit (5.0 vs 2.0), cost at your scale (4.2 vs 3.2); MongoDB is stronger on team skill match (4.0 vs 1.5), scalability (5.0 vs 4.0); MongoDB takes a penalty: Only 2/5 fit for your primary 'relational' data.
Ruled out: Eventually consistent; cannot be the system of record for ACID data; In-memory store: ~34 GB within 12 months cannot sensibly live in RAM as the system of record (use it as a cache)
Ruled out: Eventually consistent; cannot be the system of record for ACID data

tradeoffs: Team skill match is only 1.5/5 (weight 3.5).
Single-writer primary: write scale-out needs sharding (Citus) or Aurora Limitless
Connection-per-process model needs PgBouncer/RDS Proxy under serverless

hosting.choice: DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs), region BLR1 (Bangalore)
hosting.justification: DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) hosts the stack for users in India at a 99.9% availability target. It runs the Python + Django API as long-running processes with WebSockets, sized for ~12 requests/s at peak. It has a region in India, so data can stay in the country. Its share of the estimated bill is $75-$233 a month, against a total budget of $150 a month. It leads the runner-up, Google Cloud Run, by 1.0 stack points.

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 1.0 points. DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) is stronger on cost at your scale (3.9 vs 3.5), realtime fit (4.0 vs 3.0); Google Cloud Run is stronger on scalability (5.0 vs 4.0), performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 5.1 points. DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) is stronger on realtime fit (4.0 vs 2.0), portability (low lock-in) (4.0 vs 3.0); Vercel is stronger on learning curve (5.0 vs 4.0), performance / latency (5.0 vs 3.0). A stack compatibility rule costs it 6.2 points, more than the whole gap, while on this layer's own criteria it is 1.2 points ahead: Frontend platforms run code only as short-lived functions; this framework expects a long-running server. Host the API on a container/PaaS service instead.

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 5.5 points. DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs) is stronger on team skill match (3.5 vs 1.5), low ops burden (5.0 vs 3.0); AWS ECS on Fargate is stronger on ecosystem maturity (5.0 vs 4.0), scalability (5.0 vs 4.0). 1.0 of the 5.5 points come from a stack compatibility rule: Git-push deploys with managed database add-ons are the shortest path to production for a monolith.
Ruled out: No India region; data must stay in India

tradeoffs: Fewer managed services than hyperscalers

supporting.choice: WebSockets in the Python + Django app (Django Channels)
supporting.justification: Chat and live updates for a part of the product: the app server holds the connections itself; add Redis pub/sub only when a second instance must reach the same users. Up to 800 users online at once (scale.peak_concurrent_users) hold open connections.

alternatives.choice: Polling the API every few seconds
alternatives.why_not: Every client asks again and again, which multiplies requests and still shows changes late

tradeoffs: Open connections hold memory per user and need pub/sub to reach users on other instances

supporting.justification: Send emails, process uploads and call slow APIs outside the request path. Celery with a Redis broker (or RQ / Dramatiq) keeps its jobs in Redis, so the app needs a Redis/Valkey instance (DigitalOcean Managed Caching (Valkey)). Sized for the 30,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.choice: Doing the work inside the web request
alternatives.why_not: Slow emails, uploads and API calls would hold the request open and fail with it

tradeoffs: A job can run twice after a retry, so handlers must be idempotent

supporting.justification: About 34 GB of data in a year fits the database's own text index; a separate search cluster would add a second system and its bill before it is needed. Move to Meilisearch past ~100 GB or when facets and typo tolerance matter. The scenario stores 50 GB within 12 months (scale.data_volume_gb_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: A second system to run before the data needs it
They scan every row, rank nothing and miss misspellings

tradeoffs: The index is a second copy of the data and lags the database by the sync delay

supporting.choice: DigitalOcean Spaces in BLR1 (Bangalore), a private bucket with short-lived signed URLs (no public CDN)
supporting.justification: Uploaded files and video belong in object storage, not the database. Hand uploads out from the bucket, not the app server; a public CDN would cache copies at edge sites outside the country your data must stay in, and each signed URL expires within minutes. The scenario stores 50 GB within 12 months (scale.data_volume_gb_12_months).

alternatives.choice: Ceph Object Gateway on your own servers
alternatives.why_not: A storage cluster to run yourself
They bloat backups and the database disk, which costs several times more per GB than object storage

alternatives.choice: Serving files through the app server
alternatives.why_not: Each download holds an app connection and pays the app host's egress price

tradeoffs: Files and their database rows can drift apart: delete or replace both together
Links that leak can be shared until they expire, so keep their lifetime short

supporting.justification: One-time codes need an SMS gateway with rate limits against SMS-pumping fraud; Indian operators deliver only DLT-registered templates. MSG91 stores its data only in India (Google Cloud, Mumbai) according to its 2024 data-localisation audit, which notes some processing in Singapore with the data brought back to India; Twilio Verify runs in Twilio's US region (twilio.com/docs/global-infrastructure), so codes and phone numbers would be processed and stored outside India. Sized for the 30,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: Twilio runs Verify in its US region, so codes and numbers would be processed and stored outside India
Every user must install an app first, which loses sign-ups on a consumer product

tradeoffs: Each SMS is paid, and open sign-up forms invite SMS-pumping fraud: rate-limit by number and IP

supporting.justification: Card data never touches your servers, which keeps your PCI-DSS audit scope to the smallest self-assessment form (SAQ A). Stripe accepts new businesses in India by invitation only, so an Indian gateway leads. Sized for the 30,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: Equivalent hosted checkout; one gateway is enough to start
Stripe takes new Indian businesses by invitation only

alternatives.choice: Taking card details on your own pages
alternatives.why_not: Card data on your servers moves the PCI-DSS audit from the shortest self-assessment (SAQ A) to a full one

tradeoffs: Every transaction pays the gateway's fee, and refunds and disputes follow its process

supporting.choice: Django's built-in authentication (django.contrib.auth), with the users in your database in India
supporting.justification: Do not hand-roll password storage, MFA or SSO. Sized for the 30,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: A server to run, patch and back up, for no feature this project needs
Password storage, MFA, resets and lockouts are easy to get wrong and are the first things attackers test

tradeoffs: Sign-in depends on the identity provider staying up; moving users off it later is a migration

supporting.justification: Standard channel for mobile engagement on Android and iOS. Notification text leaves your residency region: Firebase Cloud Messaging may process messages anywhere Google has facilities, so send only an ID and let the app fetch the content from your servers in the region. Sized for the 30,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: It drains batteries and still misses users who are not in the app

tradeoffs: Delivery is best-effort, and users can switch notifications off

supporting.choice: OpenTelemetry instrumentation -> the host's built-in metrics and logs, kept in your Indian region; self-hosted Grafana + Prometheus + Loki there once you outgrow them
supporting.justification: Traces, metrics and error tracking from day one; required to defend an availability target. A 99.9% availability target (requirements.availability) allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month, so failures must show within minutes.

alternatives.why_not: Without traces and metrics there is no way to see which call is slow or failing

tradeoffs: Telemetry volume is billed: sample traces and set log retention

supporting.justification: Every push runs the tests and deploys the same way; hosted runners mean no build server to operate. All 3 engineers (team.size) release through the same pipeline.

alternatives.why_not: Equivalent pipelines; one more tool to learn for no gain here

tradeoffs: Pipeline minutes are metered on hosted runners

assumptions: Planning estimate from published price bands at your scale tier, each read where the project sits inside its tier, with the usage terms listed per line; excludes salaries, third-party SaaS (auth, email, payments fees) and egress spikes.
Scale tier: Medium (500-5,000 users online at once)
Budget check: $150/month stated, status 'over'

Hosting: DigitalOcean (App Platform + Managed DBs): $75-233 (Medium (500-5,000 users online at once) price band, from the band's floor up to its price at ~3x the load, for 800 users online at once (20% of the way up the tier, log scale); x1.5 for 99.9% availability (redundant instances))

Database: PostgreSQL: $75-150 (Medium (500-5,000 users online at once) database tier (~34 GB in 12 months), from the band's floor up to its price at ~3x the load, for ~34 GB of data (the bottom of the tier: that measure alone is below it); upper end for ~34 GB of data: the band's top is priced for the largest data of the tier; priced as DigitalOcean Managed PostgreSQL; x1.5 for 99.9% availability (standby/replicas))

Background jobs: Redis / Valkey: $30-114 (Medium (500-5,000 users online at once) price band (the app's scale), from the band's floor up to its price at ~3x the load, for 800 users online at once (20% of the way up the tier, log scale))

Object storage: $0-0 (~16 GB of uploaded files (the stated total less the database's ~34 GB) at $0.015-0.025/GB-month (https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing/ and https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/))
Media delivery: $9-81 (~900 GB served a month (5 MB per active user a day) at $0.01-0.09/GB)
Phone login (SMS OTP): $18-45 (~9,000 SMS a month (one login every ~20 days per active user) at $0.002-0.005 each)

warnings.message: Budget below estimated cost. Estimated minimum spend $207/month exceeds your budget of $150/month at Medium (500-5,000 users online at once) scale. Card payments: the hosted checkout collects card numbers on the payment provider's page, so your PCI DSS check is the shortest self-assessment (SAQ A). Putting card fields on your own pages, or storing card numbers, widens the audit.

compliance: DPDP Act 2023 (in force through the DPDP Rules 2025, notified November 2025 and phased in over 18 months) allows cross-border transfer except to notified countries, so it adds consent/breach-notice duties but not an India-region filter. Set infrastructure.data_residency to india if a sector rule (e.g. RBI) applies.

Stored data: The stated 50 GB counts uploaded files too. The database is sized for ~34 GB of rows (0.5 MB per daily user a month for this app type, at ~5,335 daily users, launch plus 12 months), and the other ~16 GB of files is priced as object storage on the stack's cloud.
